subject: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model

messages.author: d64b86e77132af93
messages.subject: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model
parts:
I have converted a GLM type model from JAGS to NIMBLE syntax. The model runs successfully with no errors, but the NIMBLE sample sizes are 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than JAGS.  I have tried block sampling on some of the obvious choices but not seeing any improvement.  I can see that JAGS is using slicer and conjugate normal samplers, so my next notion was to try and set the same samplers up in NIMBLE.  If there a more efficient way to at least get closer to the JAGS ESS?

BTW - love the new NIMBLE cheat sheet!

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model
parts:
Mike, when you configure the MCMC, usually a step using configureMCMC(), you could try adding the option:
configureMCMC(model, onlySlice = TRUE)

This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.

That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).

But anyway, give the slice samplers a try, and hopefully that will raise up the ESS values you're getting.

messages.subject: Re: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model

Thanks for your reply, Daniel.  I attended the recent NIMBLE workshop and recall the discussion about MCMC efficiency.  As far as a 'best practice', we have traditionally adopted the guidance found in Kruschke's book and blog, where he suggests an ESS of at least 10,000. Certainly, the diagnostics plots look convincing with multiple chains at that level of ESS, which helps to sell the approach to those less familiar Bayesian modeling.  I will take another look at MCMC efficiency as a metric going forward.

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model
parts:
Hi Mike,

Let me chime in with a couple of notes.

It is more important for NIMBLE than for JAGS to provide sensible and complete inits.  If you are not doing that, it could explain some degree of worse performance of NIMBLE.  That could be one source of the slice sampler warnings you saw.

It is also important to recognize there are relatively simple special cases where JAGS is at its best relative to NIMBLE, and simple lms and glms may potentially be those cases, anecdotally.

-Perry

Thanks for the chime, Perry. My model is fully initialized and I am using the same initialization function with both NIMBLE and JAGS. Still, I will review the initial values, as you suggested.  

I was thinking of posting a minimal example, but would need to simplify the model before doing so. Although it is not as advanced as some of your ecological models, I do not consider it a simple GLM, with 1,305 observed stochastic nodes, 2,430 unobserved stochastic nodes and a graph size of 35.564. Perhaps the real answer is that we need to work on the parameterization. 

We are working with NIMBLE because there are opportunities with user-defined distributions that we need to explore, so we're not ready to give up yet.

messages.author: d64b86e77132af93
messages.subject: Re: Very low ESS on converted JAGS model
parts:
Daniel / Perry,

We appear to have resolved the problem, with your help of course.  After I responded to Perry's post, where I indicated that a large proportion of our data is censored, it occurred to me that the censoring vector (from dinterval) was treated as data, as opposed to constants.  Moving the censoring vector to constants brought the ESS much closer to JAGS.  Once that was completed, blocking improvements were also more successful.  Additionally, we saw ESS improvements when providing a better initial value for one parameter.  As Perry indicated, the slice sampler warnings disappeared after the initial value was improved for that parameter.    

Daniel's suggestion to use 'onlySlice = TRUE' did indeed increase the ESS,  but significantly increased the runtime, as expected.  

I feel like we have a good starting point now, and can work toward further MCMC improvements.

Thanks, Mike

I ran our model, which has a large proportion of censored data 10 times and calculated the min efficiency for both cases. These results (shown below) indicate that there is no significant difference in efficiency with the censoring vector as constants vs. data. I would have to retrace our steps again, but perhaps we had a change in initial values that caused our ESS improvement. We are currently close in ESS between JAGS and NIMBLE, but as you can see the MCMC efficiency is low.

This will assign slice samplers for all non-conjugate scalar nodes in your model, very nearly replicating (with a few possible exceptions) the sampler assignments used by JAGS.

That said; it's not *all* about ESS.  The slice sampling will (generally) give higher ESS, but at the expense of a longer MCMC runtime.  We usually consider "MCMC efficiency" (which we define as min(ESS) / runtime, where the min() is taken across the sampled parameters) as the metric of how well an MCMC is doing, because that truly reflects how large an ESS you can generate, per unit runtime of MCMC sampling (for the slowest mixing model parameter).

But anyway, give the slice samplers a try, and hopefully that will raise up the ESS values you're getting.



On Wed, Jun 24, 2020 at 4:18 PM MIke Sparago <mikes...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have converted a GLM type model from JAGS to NIMBLE syntax. The model runs successfully with no errors, but the NIMBLE sample sizes are 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than JAGS.  I have tried block sampling on some of the obvious choices but not seeing any improvement.  I can see that JAGS is using slicer and conjugate normal samplers, so my next notion was to try and set the same samplers up in NIMBLE.  If there a more efficient way to at least get closer to the JAGS ESS?

parts:
To follow up on this on the list (after an exchange between Mike and
me off-list), if you use dinterval, e.g.,

for(i in 1:n)
y_cens[i] ~ dinterval(y[i], c[i])

Then `y_cens` should be specified as 'data'. If you specify it as
'constants', nimble will convert to 'data' behind the scenes.

'c' can be specified either constants if the values of 'c' are indeed
fixed. If 'c' has a prior, then one would specify its values via
'inits'.
If 'c' only appears on the right-hand side (i.e., it has no prior) but
you may want to change the values, you can specify its values either
via 'inits' or 'data'.

-Chris
